sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: See where Harvard Law's interior scenes were actually filmed.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Harvard's Admissions Boardroom wasn't filmed at Harvard.

factBeats.text: The interior scenes of Harvard University, including classrooms and this admissions boardroom, were not filmed at the actual Harvard campus.
Instead, many of the college's hallways and classrooms, including those depicting Harvard, were filmed at Rose City High School in Pasadena, California.
Harvard University generally does not permit commercial film shooting on its campus, citing potential disruption.
Ironically, while USC and UCLA refused to allow their names to be used in the film, both campuses were utilized to shoot many of the Harvard-based scenes.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: What inspired Elle's iconic pink pen?

factBeats.text: The author of the Legally Blonde novel, Amanda Brown, wrote her manuscript using a pink furry pen.
Brown claimed an agent picked her book out of a slush pile solely because it was on pink paper.
In the film, Elle's furry, glittery pen embodies her loud femininity on her first day of law school.
While other students use laptops, Elle uses her pen to take notes in a tiny heart-shaped pink notebook.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Discover the story behind Elle's bunny costume.
sceneFacts.factHeader: Elle's Iconic Bunny Costume Had a Surprising Origin

factBeats.text: Costume designer Sophie de Rakoff considers Elle's bunny costume to have the most surprising story among all the film's outfits.
The famous ensemble was created in the stockroom of an intimates shop called Trashy Lingerie.
De Rakoff conducted fittings for the costume in the back room of the shop, amidst bras and other customers.
The shop specifically built the bunny outfit for the costume designer.

factBeats.text: The prevalence of computers in the film's Harvard Law classrooms struck one real Harvard Law student as unusual.
This student, who attended the school 16 years after Elle Woods, was only allowed to use a laptop in two of their nine first-year courses.
They also doubted that professors were more "tech-friendly" in 2004, implying the film's depiction might not be accurate for its time.

sceneFacts.proactivePrompt: Discover how this iconic move came to life.
sceneFacts.factHeader: The 'Bend and Snap' was a spontaneous invention

factBeats.text: Screenwriters Kirsten Smith and Karen McCullah initially considered a crime plot for Paulette's storyline in the nail salon.
Karen McCullah then suggested that Elle could teach Paulette a move to get the UPS guy's attention.
Kirsten Smith spontaneously demonstrated the "bend and snap" move, describing its invention as a "drunken moment in a bar."
Director Robert Luketic decided to expand the move into a full musical number for the film.
